at starte på.explanation: "At starte på" means "to start on". To say you begin a task, put "på" (on) before the task: "Jeg starter på opgaven" (I start on the assignment). To say an engine or a machine starts, use "at starte" (to start) without "på": "Bilen starter ikke" (The car does not start).

at stave.explanation: "At stave" means "to spell". To ask someone how a word is spelled, use it with "man" (one): "Hvordan staver man det?" (How do you spell that?)

at stege.explanation: "At stege" means "to fry, to roast". To say you cook meat in a pan, say: "Jeg steger kød i panden" (I fry meat in the pan). To say you cook a duck in the oven, say: "Vi steger en and i ovnen" (We roast a duck in the oven). To cook in water, use "at koge" (to boil): "Jeg koger kartofler" (I boil potatoes).

at stemme.explanation: "At stemme" means "to vote". To say who you vote for, add "på" (on): "Jeg stemmer på ham" (I vote for him). To say a fact is correct, use the same verb: "Det stemmer!" (That is right!)

at stemme på.explanation: "At stemme på" means "to vote for". To name the person or party you choose, put it after "på" (on), where English says "for": "Vi stemte på Peter" (We voted for Peter).

at stige.explanation: "At stige" means "to rise / climb". To say a price goes up, say: "Prisen stiger" (The price is rising). To say you climb stairs, add "op ad" (up along): "Han stiger op ad trappen" (He climbs up the stairs). To say you get into a car, add "ind" (in): "Hun steg ind i bilen" (She got into the car).

at stige af.explanation: "At stige af" means "to get off". To say you leave a bus, a train or a bike, put "af" (off) after the verb: "Hun stiger af cyklen" (She gets off the bike). To say the opposite, use "at stige på" (to get on): "Jeg stiger på bussen" (I get on the bus).

at stige på.explanation: "At stige på" means "to get on". To say you board a bus, a train or a bike, put "på" (on) after the verb: "Vi stiger på toget i Odense" (We get on the train in Odense). To say the opposite, use "at stige af" (to get off): "Hun stiger af toget" (She gets off the train).

at stikke.explanation: "At stikke" means "to stick / sting". To say an insect stings you, say: "Bien stak mig" (The bee stung me). To say you push something into a place, add "i" (in): "Jeg stikker pengene i lommen" (I stick the money in my pocket).

at stikke af.explanation: "At stikke af" means "to run off". It is built from "at stikke" (to stick) and "af" (off). To tell what a thief did, say: "Tyven stak af" (The thief ran off).

at stikke en finger i jorden.explanation: "At stikke en finger i jorden" means "take stock". Literally, it is "to stick a finger in the ground".

at stikke en kæp i hjulet.explanation: "At stikke en kæp i hjulet" means "throw a wrench in the works". Literally, it is "to stick a stick in the wheel". To name the person whose plan you spoil, add "for" (for) and the person: "Jeg vil ikke stikke en kæp i hjulet for dig" (I do not want to spoil things for you).

at stille.explanation: "At stille" means "to put / place (upright)". To put something that stands, like a bottle, on a table, say: "Jeg stiller flasken på bordet" (I put the bottle on the table). To put something flat, like a book, use "at lægge" (to lay): "Jeg lægger bogen på bordet" (I put the book on the table).

at stille et spørgsmål.explanation: "At stille et spørgsmål" means "to ask a question". Literally, it is "to put a question". To ask a person directly, use "at spørge" (to ask): "Jeg vil spørge dig om noget" (I want to ask you something).

at stille op.explanation: "At stille op" means "to run (for office)". To say someone puts their name forward in an election, say: "Han stiller op for partiet" (He runs for the party). To say a team turns up to play, say: "Holdet stiller op til kampen" (The team turns out for the match). To say people line up, add "sig" (oneself): "Børnene stiller sig op i en række" (The children line up in a row).

at stille uret.explanation: "At stille uret" means "to set the clock". To say you move the clock ahead, add "en time frem" (an hour forward): "Vi stiller uret en time frem" (We set the clock an hour forward).

at stimulere.explanation: "At stimulere" means "to stimulate". To say you boost the economy, put "økonomien" (the economy) after it: "at stimulere økonomien" (to stimulate the economy).

at stirre.explanation: "At stirre" means "to stare". To name what you stare at, use "på" (at): "Hun stirrer på skærmen" (She stares at the screen). To say you stare into space, use "ud i luften" (out into the air): "Han stirrer ud i luften" (He stares into space).

at stjæle.explanation: "At stjæle" means "to steal". To say something was taken from you, say: "Nogen stjal min cykel" (Someone stole my bicycle). To say someone robbed a bank, use "at røve" (to rob): "Han røvede banken" (He robbed the bank).

at stole på.explanation: "At stole på" means "to trust". To say you trust someone, put "på" (on) before the person: "Jeg stoler på min læge" (I trust my doctor). In a sentence with "ikke" (not), "ikke" goes between the two words: "Jeg stoler ikke på ham" (I do not trust him).

at stoppe.explanation: "At stoppe" means "to stop". To say you quit doing something, add "med at" (with to) and a verb: "Jeg stopper med at spise slik" (I stop eating candy).

at straffe.explanation: "At straffe" means "to punish". To say what someone is punished for, add "for" (for): "Han blev straffet for sin fejl" (He was punished for his mistake).

at stramme.explanation: "At stramme" means "to tighten". To tighten a screw, say: "Jeg strammer skruen" (I tighten the screw). To say rules become stricter, say: "at stramme reglerne" (to make the rules stricter).

at streame.explanation: "At streame" means "to stream". The Danish verb is borrowed from the English word "stream".

at strejke.explanation: "At strejke" means "to strike", as in stopping work as a protest. To say the teachers are on strike, say: "Lærerne strejker" (The teachers are on strike). The noun is "strejke" (strike): "Der er strejke på skolen i dag" (There is a strike at the school today).

at strikke.explanation: "At strikke" means "to knit". To mix it up with the other yarn craft, use "at hækle" (to crochet): "Jeg hækler et tæppe" (I crochet a blanket).

at stryge.explanation: "At stryge" means "to iron". To say you iron clothes, say: "Jeg stryger tøj" (I iron clothes). To say you stroke a pet, use the same verb: "Hun stryger katten" (She strokes the cat).

at stræbe.explanation: "At stræbe" means "to strive". To name the goal you strive for, use "efter" (after): "stræbe efter succes" (to strive for success). The adjective "stræbsom" (ambitious) comes from the same verb.

at strække.explanation: "At strække" means "to stretch". To say you stretch something out, say: "Han strækker armene" (He stretches his arms). To say you stretch your own body, add "sig" (oneself): "Katten strækker sig" (The cat stretches).

at strække sig.explanation: "At strække sig" means "to stretch". To say you stretch after a workout, say: "Han strækker sig efter træning" (He stretches after exercise). The small word "sig" (oneself) changes with who stretches: "vi strækker os" (we stretch).

at strø.explanation: "At strø" means "to sprinkle / scatter". To say someone spends money freely, add "om sig" (around oneself): "Han strør om sig med penge" (He throws money around).

at studere.explanation: "At studere" means "to study". To say what someone is studying to become, use "at læse til" (literally, to read for): "Hun læser til læge" (She is studying to be a doctor).

related.en: a study, a course of study

at styre.explanation: "At styre" means "to control / steer". To say you run a company, say: "Han styrer firmaet" (He runs the company).

at styrke.explanation: "At styrke" means "to strengthen". To say something made a friendship stronger, say: "Turen styrkede venskabet" (The trip strengthened the friendship).

at styrte.explanation: "At styrte" means "to rush / crash". To say you hurry somewhere, use it with no "ned" (down): "Jeg styrtede hjem" (I rushed home). To say something falls or crashes, add "ned": "Flyet styrtede ned" (The plane crashed).

at stå.explanation: "At stå" means "to stand". To say where something upright is, say: "Flasken står på bordet" (The bottle is on the table). To say what is written somewhere, say: "Der står et navn på døren" (There is a name on the door).

at stå af.explanation: "At stå af" means "to get off". To say you leave a train, say: "Hun står af toget i Aarhus" (She gets off the train in Aarhus). For a bike, use "at stige af" (to get off): "Hun stiger af cyklen" (She gets off the bike).

at stå for.explanation: "At stå for" means "to be in charge of". To say you handle a job, say: "Jeg står for maden" (I am in charge of the food). To ask what an abbreviation means, use the same words: "Hvad står DSB for?" (What does DSB stand for?)

at stå i kø.explanation: "At stå i kø" means "to stand in line". To say traffic is jammed, use "kø" (line) alone: "Der er kø på motorvejen" (There is a traffic jam on the highway).

at stå op.explanation: "At stå op" means "to get up", as in getting out of bed. It is built from "at stå" (to stand) and "op" (up). To say you stand up from a chair, use "at rejse sig" (to stand up): "Han rejser sig fra stolen" (He stands up from the chair).

at stå på ski.explanation: "At stå på ski" means "to ski". Literally, it is "to stand on skis". To say you water ski, use "vandski" (water ski) in place of "ski": "Jeg står på vandski" (I water ski).

at støde på.explanation: "At støde på" means "to come across". To say you meet a person by chance, say: "Jeg stødte på min gamle lærer i byen" (I came across my old teacher in town). To say you face a difficulty, say: "Vi stødte på modstand" (We met resistance).

at stønne.explanation: "At stønne" means "to groan". To name what you groan about, use "over" (about): "stønne over varmen" (to groan about the heat).

at støtte.explanation: "At støtte" means "to support". To say you back a project, say: "Vi støtter projektet" (We support the project). To say you lean on something, add "sig til" (oneself on): "Han støttede sig til væggen" (He leaned on the wall).

at støve af.explanation: "At støve af" means "to dust". To say what you dust, put the things before "af" (off): "Jeg støver hylderne af" (I dust the shelves). To say you refresh an old skill, say: "støve sit fransk af" (to dust off your French).

at støvsuge.explanation: "At støvsuge" means "to vacuum". It is built from "støv" (dust) and "at suge" (to suck), and the machine is "en støvsuger" (a vacuum cleaner).

at suge.explanation: "At suge" means "to suck". To name what you suck on, use "på" (on): "Babyen suger på sutten" (The baby sucks on the pacifier). The noun "en støvsuger" (a vacuum cleaner) is built from "støv" (dust) and this verb.

at sukke.explanation: "At sukke" means "to sigh". To name what you sigh about, use "over" (about): "Hun sukker over vejret" (She sighs about the weather). The noun is "et suk" (a sigh).

at sulte.explanation: "At sulte" means "to starve". To say you are simply hungry, use "sulten" (hungry) instead: "Jeg er sulten" (I am hungry).

at summe.explanation: "At summe" means "to buzz". To say a place is full of life, say: "Byen summer af liv" (The city buzzes with life). To hum a tune, use "at nynne" (to hum): "Hun nynner en melodi" (She hums a tune).

at supplere.explanation: "At supplere" means "to supplement". To say two people each add what the other lacks, add "hinanden" (each other): "De supplerer hinanden" (They complement each other).

at sutte.explanation: "At sutte" means "to suck". To name what you suck on, use "på" (on): "Babyen sutter på flasken" (The baby sucks on the bottle).

at svare.explanation: "At svare" means "to answer". To answer a letter or a message, add "på" (on): "Hun svarer på brevet" (She answers the letter). To answer a person, name the person with no "på": "Jeg svarer ham" (I answer him).

at svare igen.explanation: "At svare igen" means "to talk back". The word "igen" means "again" in "gør det igen" (do it again), but here it means "back". To tell a child not to talk back, say: "Svar ikke igen!" (Do not talk back!)

at svare på.explanation: "At svare på" means "to answer / reply to". To reply to a message, put the message after "på" (on): "Jeg svarer på din besked" (I reply to your message).

at svede.explanation: "At svede" means "to sweat". To say someone is worried about something, add "over" (over): "Hun sveder over eksamen" (She is sweating over the exam).

at svigte.explanation: "At svigte" means "to let down / fail". To say a friend let you down, say: "Han svigtede mig" (He let me down). To say a machine failed when you needed it, say: "Bremserne svigtede" (The brakes failed).

at svinge.explanation: "At svinge" means "to swing". To say something moves back and forth, say: "Pendulet svinger" (The pendulum swings). To say you turn a corner while driving or biking, say: "Jeg svinger til højre" (I turn right).

at svække.explanation: "At svække" means "to weaken". The opposite is "at styrke" (to strengthen): "Træning styrker kroppen" (Exercise strengthens the body).

at sværge.explanation: "At sværge" means "to swear (promise)". To say you promise something is true, say: "Jeg sværger, at det er sandt" (I swear it is true). For bad language, use "at bande" (to curse): "Han bander, når han bliver vred" (He curses when he gets angry).

at svømme.explanation: "At svømme" means "to swim". To say you go for a dip in a lake or the sea, use "at bade" (to bathe): "Vi bader i søen" (We are going for a swim in the lake).

at sy.explanation: "At sy" means "to sew". To say a doctor closes a cut, use the same verb: "Lægen syede såret" (The doctor stitched the wound).

at sygemelde sig.explanation: "At sygemelde sig" means "to call in sick". It is built from "syg" (sick) and "at melde" (to report). The small word "sig" (oneself) changes with who calls in sick: "vi sygemelder os" (we call in sick).

at symbolisere.explanation: "At symbolisere" means "to symbolize". To say what a thing stands for, put the symbol first and the idea second: "Duen symboliserer fred" (The dove symbolizes peace).

at synes.explanation: "At synes" means "to think (an opinion)". To say what your opinion is, say: "Jeg synes, det er godt" (I think it is good). To ask for someone's opinion, ask: "Hvad synes du?" (What do you think?) To say you guess a fact, use "at tro" (to believe): "Jeg tror, han kommer" (I think he is coming).

at synge.explanation: "At synge" means "to sing". To say you join in a song, add "med" (with): "Jeg synger med" (I sing along).

at synke.explanation: "At synke" means "to sink / swallow". To say a ship goes down, say: "Skibet synker" (The ship sinks). To say food or a pill goes down your throat, say: "Jeg kan ikke synke tabletten" (I cannot swallow the pill).

at såre.explanation: "At såre" means "to hurt / wound". To say you hurt someone's feelings, say: "Hun sårede mig" (She hurt me). To say something hurts in the body, use "at gøre ondt" (to hurt): "Det gør ondt" (It hurts).

at sælge.explanation: "At sælge" means "to sell". To say something is for sale, use "til salg" (for sale): "Bilen er til salg" (The car is for sale).

at sænke.explanation: "At sænke" means "to lower". To say you speak more quietly, say: "Han sænker stemmen" (He lowers his voice). To say someone sinks a ship on purpose, say: "Piraterne sænker skibet" (The pirates sink the ship). When something goes down by itself, use "at synke" (to sink): "Skibet synker" (The ship sinks).

at sætte.explanation: "At sætte" means "to put / place". To say you put something on a shelf, say: "Jeg sætter bogen på hylden" (I put the book on the shelf). To tell someone to sit down, add "dig" (yourself): "Sæt dig" (Sit down). To say where you already are sitting, use "at sidde" (to sit): "Jeg sidder på stolen" (I sit on the chair).

at sætte i gang.explanation: "At sætte i gang" means "to start / launch". To say you launch a project, say: "Vi sætter projektet i gang" (We are launching the project). When something starts without anyone starting it, use "at komme i gang" (to get going): "Projektet kommer i gang" (The project gets going).

at sætte ind.explanation: "At sætte ind" means "to put in / deposit". To say you put money in the bank, say: "Jeg sætter pengene ind på kontoen" (I put the money into the account). To say you start using more of something, say: "Vi sætter flere busser ind" (We are putting more buses into service).

at sætte pris på.explanation: "At sætte pris på" means "to appreciate". Literally, it is "to put a price on". To say you appreciate something a lot, put "stor" (big) before "pris": "Jeg sætter stor pris på det" (I really appreciate it).

at sætte på.explanation: "At sætte på" means "to put on". To say you start music or a pot of coffee, say: "Jeg sætter musik på" (I put some music on). For clothes, use "at tage på" (to put on): "Jeg tager jakken på" (I put on the jacket).

at sætte sig.explanation: "At sætte sig" means "to sit down". To say you take a seat, say: "Jeg sætter mig i sofaen" (I sit down on the sofa). To say where you already are sitting, use "at sidde" (to sit): "Jeg sidder i sofaen" (I am sitting on the sofa).

related.en: a seat (the part you sit on)

at søge.explanation: "At søge" means "to search / apply". To say you apply for a job, say: "Jeg søger et job" (I am applying for a job). To say you search for something, add "efter" (for): "Jeg søger efter mine nøgler" (I am searching for my keys).

at søge efter.explanation: "At søge efter" means "to search for". To say you apply for a job, leave out "efter" (for) and use "at søge" (to apply): "Hun søger et job" (She is applying for a job).

at søge ind på.explanation: "At søge ind på" means "to apply to (a school)". To say you apply for a job, use "at søge" (to apply) without "ind på": "Hun søger et job" (She is applying for a job).

at søge job.explanation: "At søge job" means "to apply for a job". To say you are looking for work, say: "Jeg søger job som lærer" (I am looking for a job as a teacher). To say you apply for one position, use "at søge en stilling" (to apply for a position): "Han søger en stilling i banken" (He is applying for a position at the bank).

at søge om.explanation: "At søge om" means "to apply for". To say you ask an office for something, put the thing after "om" (for): "søge om tilladelse" (apply for a permit). To say you apply for a job, use "at søge" (to apply) without "om": "Hun søger et job" (She is applying for a job).

at sørge for.explanation: "At sørge for" means "to make sure / take care of". To say you handle something, say: "Jeg sørger for maden" (I take care of the food). To tell someone to make sure of something, say: "Sørg for at låse døren" (Make sure you lock the door).

en sadel.explanation: "En sadel" means "a saddle". To talk about the seat of a bike, use the same word: "Sadlen på min cykel er for høj" (The seat on my bike is too high).

en sag.explanation: "En sag" means "a matter / case". To say something is a separate issue, say: "Det er en anden sag" (That is a different matter). To say a lawyer works on a legal case, say: "Advokaten arbejder på en sag" (The lawyer is working on a case).

en sagsbehandler.explanation: "En sagsbehandler" means "a caseworker". It is built from "en sag" (a case) and "at behandle" (to handle).

en saks.explanation: "En saks" means "a pair of scissors". To ask to borrow one pair, say: "Kan jeg låne din saks?" (Can I borrow your scissors?)

en sal.explanation: "En sal" means "a hall", as in a large room for events. For the hallway of a home, use "en gang" (a hallway): "Skoene står i gangen" (The shoes are in the hallway).

en salamander.explanation: "En salamander" means "a salamander". To say what its skin is like, say: "En salamander har fugtig hud" (A salamander has moist skin). Do not mix it up with "et firben" (a lizard): "Firbenet har skæl" (The lizard has scales).

en salat.explanation: "En salat" means "a salad / lettuce". To talk about a dish, say: "Jeg spiser en salat til frokost" (I eat a salad for lunch). To talk about the plant from the shop, use "en hovedsalat" (a head of lettuce): "Jeg køber en hovedsalat" (I buy a head of lettuce).

en saltbøsse.explanation: "En saltbøsse" means "a salt shaker". To ask for it at the table, say: "Kan du række mig saltbøssen?" (Can you pass me the salt shaker?)

en salve.explanation: "En salve" means "an ointment". To say you have one at home, say: "Jeg har en salve i skabet" (I have an ointment in the cupboard). The same word also means a volley: "en salve skud" (a volley of shots).

en samlever.explanation: "En samlever" means "a live-in partner". It is built from "sammen" (together) and "at leve" (to live).

en samling.explanation: "En samling" means "a collection". To talk about circle time at kindergarten, use "samling" with no "en": "Vi har samling klokken ti" (We have circle time at ten).

en sammenhæng.explanation: "En sammenhæng" means "a connection". To say "in that context", use the phrase "i den sammenhæng": "I den sammenhæng er det vigtigt" (In that context it is important).

en sammenkomst.explanation: "En sammenkomst" means "a get-together". It is built from "sammen" (together) and "at komme" (to come). For a party, use "en fest" (a party): "Vi holder fest i aften" (We are having a party tonight).

en sammenligning.explanation: "En sammenligning" means "a comparison". To name the two things you compare, use "mellem" (between): "en sammenligning mellem to byer" (a comparison between two cities).

en sammensværgelse.explanation: "En sammensværgelse" means "a conspiracy". It is built from "sammen" (together) and "at sværge" (to swear).

en samtale.explanation: "En samtale" means "a conversation". It is built from "sam-" (together) and "en tale" (a talk). To say phone call, put "telefon" (phone) in front: "en telefonsamtale" (a phone call).

en samtaleøvelse.explanation: "En samtaleøvelse" means "a conversation exercise". It is built from "samtale" (conversation) and "en øvelse" (an exercise).

en samvittighed.explanation: "En samvittighed" means "a conscience". To say you have done nothing wrong, say: "Jeg har en ren samvittighed" (I have a clear conscience).
